passage:
In the hostel common room, Sumit slammed his diary shut. "Two more years of this!" he told Vikas Sir, the warden, who was stacking chairs. "Curfew, a fixed timetable, asking permission to go to the market. I want to run my own life now and be somebody."
Vikas Sir did not lecture. "That sounds like a long road," he said. "What's one thing you could own this month?"
Sumit scowled, then muttered, "Planning the Diwali fund for the hostel."
"Good. Bring me a plan by Friday."
Sumit stomped off. On Friday he came back with a page of figures, and for the first time the two years looked like a set of smaller steps.

qa.q: How many more years does Sumit say he has left in the hostel?
qa.a: Two more years.

qa.q: What is Sumit feeling as he slams his diary shut?
qa.a: Frustrated and impatient. He resents the curfew and permissions and wants to run his own life now.

qa.q: What small step turned Sumit's impatience into something workable?
qa.a: Vikas Sir asked what Sumit could own this month, and Sumit chose to plan the hostel Diwali fund and brought a plan by Friday.

qa.q: How does Vikas Sir seem to see Sumit's outburst?
qa.a: He treats it as a real feeling of a long wait and does not lecture, instead offering a concrete task that gives Sumit some ownership.

grounding: A teenager wants independence and adult status immediately, and a small milestone makes the wait tolerable.

passage:
Dear Imran Bhai,
You asked how school is. Honestly? It feels like waiting in a queue that never moves. At home everyone still treats me like a kid: no phone after nine, no travelling alone, no say in what I study. You left home at eighteen, and I want that now, not in three years.
I have started crossing off days on a calendar, which is silly, I know. Last week Papa let me plan the route for our family trip, and for three days I felt grown. Maybe the small yeses are the road.
Still, please tell me it goes faster than it feels.
Nirmala

qa.q: What did Nirmala start doing on a calendar?
qa.a: Crossing off days.

qa.q: What is Nirmala feeling about waiting to grow up?
qa.a: Impatient and restless, because home still treats Nirmala like a kid and three years feels endless.

qa.q: What made a difference to Nirmala last week?
qa.a: Papa let Nirmala plan the family trip's route, and for three days Nirmala felt grown, which suggests small milestones help.

qa.q: How might Imran feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably fond and understanding, since Imran left home at eighteen and Nirmala looks up to Imran enough to ask if the wait goes faster.

grounding: A teenager resents the wait for adult independence and finds small milestones make it bearable.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11, Tuesday.
Jagdish came in frustrated. He wants to leave home, work, earn and "start real life" now, and says school feels like "two years of waiting room". He resents his parents for saying no to a part-time job, and he has stopped doing homework as a kind of protest.
I didn't argue with the wish. It's real. Instead we broke the two years into smaller pieces he can actually reach: learn to cook three meals by Diwali, handle his own bus pass, do one weekend volunteering shift a month, finish the Class 11 exams.
He looked less angry by the end. He said, "So I'm not just waiting. I'm doing the first bits."
Follow-up in four weeks.
Madhuri

qa.q: What does Jagdish call school?
qa.a: "Two years of waiting room".

qa.q: How does Jagdish feel about his parents saying no?
qa.a: Jagdish feels resentful and frustrated, and has stopped doing homework as a protest.

qa.q: Why did breaking the wait into small goals help?
qa.a: Small reachable milestones, like cooking three meals and handling his bus pass, made the long wait feel like progress.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's parents see his homework protest?
qa.a: His parents probably see it as rebellion or worry about his marks, without seeing the impatience behind it.

grounding: Shows a teenager resenting the wait for independence, and small milestones making the long timeline bearable.

passage:
Sunday
Everyone keeps saying "when you're eighteen". When you're eighteen you can drive. When you're eighteen you can go on the Goa trip. When you're eighteen, when you're eighteen. I'm fifteen. That's three whole years. It feels like forever and I'm sick of it.
Elizabeth Didi laughed when I said that at dinner, which made it worse. But later she came to my room and showed me her old notebook from when she was fifteen. She'd made a list of small things she could do before eighteen. Learn to swim properly. Take the bus to the city alone. Cook biryani. Earn something from tuition. She'd ticked them all off.
So I made my own list. First one: take the bus to Nani's alone next month. Mummy said yes!
Vaibhav

qa.q: What is the first item on Vaibhav's list?
qa.a: Take the bus to Nani's alone next month.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav feel about waiting till eighteen?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels fed up and impatient, as if three years were forever.

qa.q: Why does the list help?
qa.a: Small milestones like the solo bus trip turn the long wait into steps Vaibhav can take now.

qa.q: Why might Elizabeth Didi have shown her old notebook?
qa.a: Elizabeth Didi probably remembered feeling the same at fifteen and wanted to help after laughing at dinner.

grounding: Shows a teenager impatient for adult freedoms, with small milestones making the long wait bearable.

passage: The bus from the kasba was late again, and Gurpreet kicked at the dust by the stop. "Two more years of this," she muttered. "Two more years before anyone lets me decide anything." At sixteen she already stitched half the salwar suits Mummy sold from their front room, yet she still had to ask before going to the market alone. Kavitha, who ran the sewing class above the post office, sat down beside her on the bench. "What do you want by then?" "My own shop. My own customers. Nobody checking on me." Kavitha pulled out an old receipt and turned it over. "Write three things you can do before Diwali." Gurpreet scowled, then wrote: take one order by myself, keep my own order book, go to the cloth wholesaler in town once with Mummy and then once alone. The bus finally came. She folded the paper into her pocket.

qa.q: What did Kavitha ask Gurpreet to write on the back of the receipt?
qa.a: She asked her to write three things she can do before Diwali.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling while she waited at the bus stop?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and resentful, kicking the dust and muttering that it would be two more years before anyone let her decide anything.

qa.q: Why might Kavitha's list help more than a talk about waiting?
qa.a: Three small steps before Diwali give Gurpreet something real to do now, so the long wait feels shorter and she still moves toward her own shop.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Gurpreet's plan to go to the wholesaler alone?
qa.a: Mummy might feel proud and a little worried at once; going together first gives her a chance to see that Gurpreet can manage.

grounding: Shows a teenager resenting a long wait for independence and a mentor turning that timeline into small milestones she can reach soon.
